common_name: Huntington Artichoke Agave (Compact Truncate Parry's Agave)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in extremely well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; this selection resents winter wet more than winter cold, so raised beds or slope plantings outperform flat, poorly drained ground.

directions: Huntington is a tight, exceptionally symmetrical selection of the truncate form of Parry's agave, its thick, cupped, pale blue-gray leaves stacked so closely that the rosette reads almost artichoke-like, each leaf tipped with a stout, curved terminal spine that emerges dark reddish-brown and fades to gray with age. It is one of the more cold-hardy ornamental agaves in cultivation, shrugging off temperatures well below freezing once established, which makes it a reliable garden specimen rather than a container-only curiosity in much of the Southwest. Like the species it is monocarpic, taking a decade or more to build its dense rosette before sending up a single branched flower spike and dying, but it offsets modestly at the base to continue the clump. Give it lean, mineral soil and keep it dry through winter, since rot from standing moisture is the far greater risk than cold.

common_name: Vanzie Whale's Tongue Agave (Scalloped-Leaf Ovatifolia Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in extremely well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; give it room to reach full width, since crowded plants lose the sweeping, upward-cupped leaf form that distinguishes this selection.

directions: Vanzie is a named clonal selection of whale's tongue agave chosen for deeply channeled, ventrally folded leaves with a more scalloped, wavy margin and smaller marginal teeth than the wild species, along with a noticeably faster growth rate to full size. The broad, powdery blue-gray leaves sweep upward and inward in a dense, architectural rosette that reads as one of the boldest specimen forms available among cold-hardy agaves. It shares the straight species' outstanding tolerance for Gulf Coast and Texas Hill Country conditions, taking summer heat, drought, and freezes into the low single digits once established, and its faster bulk-up means a garden-worthy specimen size is reached sooner than from seed-grown plants. It is monocarpic, flowering once on a tall branched stalk after a decade or more before the rosette dies, typically leaving few if any offsets, so propagation is mostly by division of nursery-produced tissue-culture stock.

common_name: Monterrey Frost Squid Agave (Variegated Frosted Candelabrum Agave)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in average, gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most agaves this pale-leaved selection scorches in the most intense afternoon sun, so light shade preserves the cleanest variegation.

directions: Monterrey Frost is a rare variegated selection of the spineless squid agave, its narrow, pliable, arching leaves colored pale green in the center with wide, creamy-white margins that give the whole rosette a frosted, pastel glow unlike any other commonly grown agave. Because the leaves carry no marginal teeth or terminal spine, it is one of the few agaves safe to plant directly beside a path or patio and to handle without gloves, and its lax, reflexed form suits rock gardens and container plantings where its unusual pale coloring can be appreciated up close. It tolerates surprisingly cold winters for such a delicate-looking plant and, like the straight species, forms offsets readily at the base, making division rather than seed the standard way to propagate true-to-type plants. Give it a bit more shade and a bit less baking sun than other agaves to prevent the white variegation from bleaching or scorching.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun; give plants a few weeks of direct sun exposure after any period indoors or under cover to restore full leaf color and spotting.

directions: Kaleidoscope is a sport of the popular Mangave 'Jaguar' selected for bold golden-yellow leaf margins surrounding a green, softly speckled center — a reversed color pattern from the similarly marked cultivar Carnival, which carries the yellow in the middle instead of at the edges. It inherits the fast growth and forgiving nature of its Manfreda parentage along with the refined rosette form of Agave, forming a rubbery-leaved clump with a softly spined border that is far less hazardous to handle than a true agave. Sun intensity drives the vividness of both the yellow variegation and the purple-red speckling that develops on the leaves, so plants kept in low light indoors or under poly through winter fade and need several weeks back in strong sun to recolor. Unlike a true agave it is not strictly monocarpic and does not require decades to reach garden size, flowering and offsetting within a few seasons while remaining an attractive foliage plant throughout.

common_name: Baby Rita Prickly Pear (Dwarf Purple-Padded Santa Rita Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant rooted pads in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; the deepest purple pad color develops under cold, dry, sun-stressed winter conditions rather than rich, moist culture.

directions: Baby Rita is a compact hybrid between the tall, shrubby Santa Rita prickly pear and the low, mat-forming beavertail prickly pear, combining the parent Santa Rita's rich winter purple pad color with a much smaller, garden-scaled habit that never needs the hard pruning a full-size Santa Rita eventually demands. The rounded, blue-gray pads flush deep amethyst-purple with cold and drought stress in fall and winter, then relax back toward soft blue-green as temperatures and moisture rise in spring, giving the plant two distinct seasonal looks from the same clump. Bright pink flowers appear in flushes from spring into summer, held just above the pads and contrasting sharply against the purple coloring when both occur together. As with other opuntias, propagate by rooting detached pads in dry soil, and keep plantings out of standing water or heavy clay, which is a far greater threat than winter cold.

common_name: Peter Pan Prickly Pear (Dwarf Juvenile Hedgehog Prickly Pear)

planting.note: Plant rooted pads in spring in lean, rocky or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; keep dry in winter dormancy, since this selection comes from a high-plains grassland climate with cold, dry winters rather than wet ones.

directions: Peter Pan is a naturally occurring dwarf, perpetually juvenile form of the widespread hedgehog prickly pear, collected from Colorado's shortgrass prairie and selected for pads that stay only a few inches across and rarely if ever flower, so the plant never grows out of its low, spiny, carpet-forming stage. Densely packed clusters of small, bright white spines cover the tightly bunched pads, creating a fine, pale, almost frosted texture that spreads slowly into a low mat rather than an upright clump. Because it comes from a cold, high-elevation grassland, it is markedly more cold-hardy than most ornamental prickly pears grown for foliage or flower, tolerating hard winter freezes with ease as long as drainage is sharp. Its scale and spreading habit suit rock gardens, troughs, and gravel beds where a true miniature cactus texture is wanted without the size of a typical flowering opuntia.
sources: Kelly Grummons / Timberline Gardens introduction records

common_name: Meat Claw Agave (Red-Spined Cabbage Head Agave Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in gritty, lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; site away from paths, since the exaggerated hooked spines are more dangerous than on the straight species.

directions: Meat Claw is a chance seedling selection of the Coahuila limestone-mountain species Agave parrasana, chosen for unusually long, wickedly hooked marginal spines that emerge bright red before aging toward gray-brown, set against rough-textured, frosty blue-gray leaves imprinted with the pattern of the leaves that once pressed against them in the bud. It stays compact and slow-growing, building a tight, symmetrical rosette over many years and rarely offsetting, which keeps it a solitary specimen rather than a spreading clump. Despite its high-elevation Mexican origin it tolerates real winter cold once established, making it one of the hardier small ornamental agaves for rock gardens and container culture in areas with occasional hard freezes. Because it offsets so sparingly, most nursery stock is produced by tissue culture rather than division, and named clones like this one should be kept true rather than grown from open-pollinated seed.

common_name: Joe Hoak Agave (Cream-Margined Smooth Agave Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; move or protect plants when temperatures approach freezing, since this selection is noticeably less cold-tolerant than most garden agaves.

directions: Joe Hoak, named for the Miami, Florida nursery credited with its origin, is a strikingly variegated selection of the spineless, smooth-edged Agave desmettiana, its wide, soft, almost rubbery leaves striped pale gray-green and cream through the center and finished with a bold dark-green margin along the lower half of each leaf. It grows and offsets quickly compared with most ornamental agaves, filling out a full-size rosette and producing pups within a few seasons rather than a decade, which makes it a fast-payoff container and landscape specimen in warm climates. Because it lacks the marginal teeth and sharp terminal spine typical of the genus, it is comfortable to site near seating areas and walkways, but its tropical origin means it is among the more cold-sensitive agaves in general cultivation and needs frost protection or container culture outside the warmest zones. Give it bright light for the most vivid variegation, since deep shade causes the cream striping to green over and lose contrast.

common_name: White Rhino Agave (Broad-Margined Queen Victoria Agave Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in gritty, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun to partial shade; keep bone-dry through winter dormancy to protect the slow-growing rosette from rot.

directions: White Rhino is a nursery-origin variegated form of the compact, sculptural queen Victoria agave, its thick, deep green leaves broadly edged in creamy white that spreads irregularly toward the leaf center, producing a rosette even more strikingly patterned than the already-ornamental straight species. It keeps the same dense, tightly packed, globe-like rosette shape and thin white leaf markings on the green portions that make victoriae-reginae one of the most collected small agaves, but with a much bolder overall variegated effect. Because such heavily variegated sports rarely breed true from seed and have proven difficult to tissue-culture, plants are propagated primarily by dividing offset-producing mature specimens, which keeps availability limited and growth exceptionally slow even by agave standards. It shares the straight species' excellent cold tolerance and dislike of wet winter soil, making sharp drainage and a dry dormant season more important to its survival than protecting it from cold alone.
